doc.title: Charles Lloyd — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Phineas Newborn and the Memphis blues circuit
title: White bands in West Memphis and Phineas's beating by police
summary: Visiting white bandsmen jam after hotel dances; a vocalist takes up with Phineas and police beat him badly.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I don’t know the chronology, but here’s the thing: We were playing over in West Memphis, and these white bands would come to the Peabody and these hotels, and they would play. Like Tex Beneke and all these players. And they had guys who wanted to jam, they wanted to cut loose after this hotel dance, playing “dah-dah-dah-dah-dah...”
So anyway. Oh, that’s one of my songs. [Laughs]
I coin-i-fied one of my songs! That was the Island Blues. [Sings melody for piece]

That goes to show, you know, don’t point no fingers. But I remember these bands would come over to play, and you know what happened to Phineas? One night this vocalist, looking like Marilyn Monroe or something was with one of those bands. They liked fine girls out front.

She came over and she heard Phineas and she said, “I gotta give him some. I just can’t help it. I just, he, you know. I may have to give it to him. All these guys in the band want to screw me, it’s like Doris Day or something, but I’m gonna give it to this guy cause he’s the one deserving it.” Somehow she made a rondeaveu with him and police found out about it, came with the billy clubs like they did to Miles and Bud Powell and stuff, and whooped the pee juice out of him, man. And that was the start of it, you know. I’m playing with Willy Mitchell across the road and across the river were Danny’s Cotton Club or somewhere, we played - this was later on, Phineas had left. Jackie Brenston had a hit, Rocket 88, and they left.
